title: Car won't start
metaDesc: Car won't start? Answer a few quick questions to see if it's the battery, starter, fuel or key, how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
synonyms: clicking when I turn the key
nothing happens when I turn the key
intro: When a car won't start, what you hear and see in the first few seconds tells you a lot. A dead battery, a failing starter and a fuel or ignition problem each behave differently. Answer the questions below and we'll point you toward the likely causes and the safest next step.
safety: If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
If you see smoke or smell burning plastic from under the hood, stop trying and step away from the car.
Don't crank the engine for more than 10 seconds at a time. Wait about a minute between tries so the starter doesn't overheat.

q_what_happens.q: What happens when you turn the key or press Start?
q_what_happens.help: "Cranking" is the whirring sound of the engine turning over (rrr-rrr-rrr) before it fires up.

opts.a: Nothing at all: no sound, and the dash stays dark
Rapid clicking or chattering (click-click-click)
One loud click, then nothing, but the dash lights come on
The engine cranks normally but never fires up
It starts, then stalls within a few seconds
I'm not sure

q_lights.q: When you turn the key to ON (or press Start without your foot on the brake), do the dash lights come on brightly?
q_lights.help: Turn the headlights on too. If they're dim or flicker when you try to start, the battery is the likely culprit.

opts.a: No, or they're very dim
Yes, bright, but the engine doesn't turn over
Yes, and the engine turns over but won't run
I'm not sure

q_jump.q: Have you tried a jump start or a battery booster?

opts.a: Yes, and it started
Yes, and it still just clicks
Not yet
I'm not sure

q_cranks_clues.help: These clues separate a fuel problem from an ignition or security problem.

opts.a: The fuel gauge is low or near empty
A key, lock or security light is flashing on the dash
I smell fuel strongly after cranking
It ran fine before, then died while driving and now won't restart
None of these / I'm not sure
Right after starting, every time
Mostly on cold mornings, then it's fine once warm
When I put it in gear or turn on the A/C
I'm not sure

result.title: The battery may be completely drained or disconnected
result.now: First look at the battery: if it's swollen, cracked, leaking, very hot or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump-start or charge it. Keep sparks away and have it checked. If it looks normal, check that the battery cables are tight and free of crusty white or green buildup, then try a jump start or a battery booster.
if: If a jump start works, drive for at least 30 minutes or have the battery and charging system tested soon, because it may die again.
If nothing at all happens even with a good jump, a main fuse, the ignition switch or a cable may have failed. Have it towed to a shop.
result.why: With no sound and no dash lights, there's essentially no electrical power reaching the car. That most often comes from a dead battery or a loose or corroded battery cable, and occasionally a blown main fuse. A battery test will confirm whether the battery itself is worn out or just drained.

causes.name: Dead or drained battery
causes.clues: Lights left on, a car that sat for weeks, a battery older than 4–5 years, or very cold weather.
causes.against: If the dash lights come on brightly, the battery is less likely to be the main problem.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on the terminals, or a cable you can wiggle by hand.

causes.name: Blown main fuse or failed ignition switch
causes.clues: A jump start changes nothing at all.
causes.against: Much less common than a battery problem.

you: Check whether the dome light and headlights work.
Look at the battery terminals for corrosion or loose clamps.
Try a jump start or a battery booster pack.
shop: Parasitic draw test if the battery keeps dying
Main fuse and ignition circuit check

result.title: Rapid clicking often means the battery is too weak to turn the starter
result.now: First look at the battery: if it's swollen, cracked, leaking, very hot or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump-start or charge it. Keep sparks away and have it checked. If it looks normal, check that the battery clamps are tight and clean, then try a jump start or a battery booster.
if: If it starts with a jump, have the battery and alternator tested soon. Most auto parts stores do this free.
If it still only clicks with a good jump, the battery cables or the starter are the more likely problem.
result.why: The starter needs a big burst of power. A weak battery has enough to light the dash and make the starter's switch click, but not enough to spin the engine, so you hear rapid clicking as it tries over and over.

causes.name: Weak or discharged battery
causes.clues: Dim lights, a slow crank in recent days, cold weather, or a battery older than 4–5 years.

causes.name: Corroded or loose battery terminal
causes.clues: Visible buildup, or the clicking changes when you wiggle a cable.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light came on while driving, or the battery keeps going flat.
causes.against: If the car started fine yesterday after a long drive, a charging fault is less likely.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Try a jump start or a booster pack.
Note whether the battery warning light came on recently while driving.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the battery cables

result.title: The battery was low. Find out why before it happens again
result.now: Keep the engine running for a while or drive it at least 30 minutes, then get the battery and charging system tested within the next few days.
if: If the battery warning light comes on while driving, pull over when it's safe and turn off everything you don't need. The alternator may not be charging, and the car could die on the road, so have it towed or checked where it is.
If the battery light comes on and the temperature gauge starts climbing, pull over and turn the engine off. On many cars one belt drives both the alternator and the water pump.
If it was a one-time mistake, like lights left on, a test will tell you if the battery recovered.
result.why: A jump start fixing it suggests the battery didn't have enough charge. The question is why: an aging battery, an alternator that isn't recharging it, or something draining it while the car is parked. A battery and charging test will usually show which before anything is replaced.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old, or the car cranks slowly on cold mornings.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light flickers or stays on, the headlights dim at idle, or there's a whining noise.

causes.name: Something draining the battery while parked
causes.clues: It keeps happening after the car sits overnight or for a few days.

you: Watch for the battery warning light while driving.
Note how old the battery is (often stamped on a label on top).

result.title: Possibly a bad battery connection or a failing starter
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean. If they are and a jump doesn't help, have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If cleaning or tightening the cables fixes it, have the cables checked for hidden corrosion soon.
If you're stuck somewhere unsafe, call roadside assistance rather than repeatedly cranking.
If a battery cable is hot to the touch, or you smell burning or see smoke, stop trying to start it and step away.
result.why: When even a good jump only produces clicking, enough power isn't reaching the starter motor. That can point to a poor connection somewhere in the heavy cables, or to a starter that's worn out. A voltage-drop test usually tells the two apart before any part is replaced.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable or ground strap
causes.clues: Buildup on the terminals, or a cable that's warm or loose.

causes.name: Failing starter motor or solenoid
causes.clues: The starter has been slow or noisy recently, or tapping it has made it work before.

causes.name: Battery with an internal fault
causes.clues: The battery is old and won't hold a charge even after charging.

you: Tighten and clean the battery clamps.
Check the ground strap from the engine to the body for a loose or broken connection.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the positive and ground cables

result.title: Possibly the starter, or a poor connection to it
result.now: Make sure the car is fully in Park (or press the clutch on a manual) and try again. If it still only clicks once, the car will need a tow or a mobile mechanic.
if: If it starts in Neutral but not Park, the gear-position (neutral safety) switch may be the problem.
If it starts after a few tries, get the starter checked soon. It may get worse.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood, stop trying and step away from the car.
result.why: Bright dash lights mean the battery has some power. One loud click often means the starter's switch (solenoid) is getting the signal but the motor isn't turning, which points to a worn starter or a bad connection to it. A shop will usually test the cables and connections before replacing the starter.

causes.name: Worn starter motor or solenoid
causes.clues: Starting has been hit-or-miss lately, or the starter sounded slow or grinding.

causes.name: Gear-position (neutral safety) or clutch switch
causes.clues: It starts in Neutral but not Park, or it depends on how you press the clutch.

causes.name: Bad cable connection at the starter
causes.clues: The problem comes and goes, especially after rain or rough roads.

you: Try starting in Neutral.
On a manual, press the clutch fully to the floor.

result.title: It may simply be out of fuel, or the gauge may be wrong
result.now: Add a few gallons of fuel and try again. On a slope, the engine may not be able to pick up the last bit of fuel in the tank.
if: If it starts after adding fuel, but the gauge showed fuel left, have the fuel gauge checked so it doesn't leave you stranded.
If it still cranks without starting after adding fuel, the fuel pump may have failed. Have it towed.
If you smell raw fuel after adding fuel or cranking, stop and look for a leak. Don't keep trying to start it.
result.why: An engine that cranks normally but never fires usually isn't getting fuel or spark. A low tank is the simplest explanation, and fuel gauges can read wrong.

causes.name: Out of fuel
causes.clues: The gauge is near empty, or the car is parked on a hill.

causes.name: Faulty fuel gauge sender
causes.clues: The gauge has acted strangely before.

causes.name: Failing fuel pump
causes.clues: Adding fuel doesn't help, and you can't hear a brief hum from the rear when you turn the key to ON.

you: Add fuel.
With the car quiet, turn the key to ON and listen for a 2-second hum from the back of the car.
shop: Fuel pump power and ground check

result.title: The anti-theft system may not be recognizing your key
result.now: Try your spare key. For push-button start, hold the key fob right against the Start button, or put it where your owner's manual says, while you press Start.
if: If the spare works, replace the battery in your main key fob or have the key checked.
If neither key works, the car may need a dealer or locksmith with the right equipment to reprogram the key.
result.why: A flashing key or security light usually means the car's immobilizer is blocking fuel or ignition because it can't read a valid key. The engine will crank but won't run until it recognizes one.

causes.name: Dead key fob battery
causes.clues: The remote's range has been getting shorter.

causes.name: Damaged or unprogrammed key
causes.clues: A new copy that wasn't programmed, or a key that's been dropped or got wet.

causes.name: Immobilizer system fault
causes.clues: Neither key works.

you: Try the spare key.
Replace the key fob battery (often a coin battery).

result.title: The engine may be flooded, or fuel may be leaking
result.now: Stop cranking. Look under the car and around the engine for wet spots or dripping fuel. If you see any, don't try to start it again and have it towed.
if: If there's no visible leak, open the hood and wait 15–20 minutes. Only if the smell has faded, try once: press the gas pedal fully to the floor and hold it while you crank for up to 10 seconds. On most fuel-injected cars this cuts fuel to help clear a flooded engine.
Not seeing a leak doesn't prove there isn't one. If the smell stays strong, comes back or gets stronger, don't crank again. Have it towed.
If it still won't start after that one try, have it towed.
result.why: A strong fuel smell after cranking can mean fuel is reaching the engine but not burning, which can flood it. It can also mean a leak, which is a fire risk.

causes.name: Flooded engine
causes.clues: Several long cranking attempts, especially on a cold engine.

causes.name: Fuel leak
causes.clues: A wet spot under the car, or a smell that's strongest near one area.

causes.name: No spark (ignition fault)
causes.clues: Fuel is getting there but nothing ignites it.

you: Look for dripping fuel or wet spots.
Don't smoke or use flames nearby.

result.title: The fuel pump or a crankshaft sensor may have failed
result.now: Don't keep cranking it. Have the car towed to a shop.
if: If it restarts after cooling down for 30 minutes or more, don't count on it. These parts can fail completely soon after, so get it checked before driving any distance.
If you heard a loud bang, rattling or knocking, or the temperature gauge was in the red before it died, don't try to restart it. Tell the shop.
If the engine sounds different when cranking, such as faster or more even than usual, stop cranking. A broken timing belt can do this.
result.why: An engine that shuts off while driving and won't restart has usually lost fuel or spark. Common causes include a fuel pump that's stopped working or a crankshaft position sensor, the part that tells the engine computer when to fire. A shop will test fuel pressure and check for codes before replacing either.

causes.name: Failed fuel pump
causes.clues: No hum from the rear when you turn the key to ON, or sputtering before it died.

causes.name: Failed crankshaft position sensor
causes.clues: It died suddenly with no sputter, and may restart once cool.

causes.name: Fuel pump relay or fuse
causes.clues: It died suddenly. These are cheap to check first.

causes.name: Broken timing belt or chain
causes.clues: The engine cranks faster or sounds different than usual, and it died suddenly.
causes.against: Less common than a fuel or sensor fault.

you: Listen for the fuel pump hum.
Note whether a check engine light came on before it died.
shop: Scan for crank and cam sensor codes
Fuel pump relay and fuse check
Timing belt or chain check if the cranking sounds unusual

result.title: The engine may not be getting fuel or spark. A shop can test it
result.now: Try once or twice more, each time for no more than 10 seconds. If it doesn't fire, have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you smell fuel or see a leak, stop trying and keep flames away.
If a check engine light is on, a code reader can give the shop a head start.
If the cranking sounds faster, uneven or different than usual, stop trying. A broken timing belt can do this and more cranking won't help.
result.why: A normal crank suggests the battery and starter are working. The engine needs fuel, spark and air at the right time to run, so one of those is likely missing. Telling which one takes a few quick tests.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem (pump, relay, filter)
causes.clues: No hum from the rear when you turn the key to ON.

causes.name: Ignition problem (sensor, coil, wiring)
causes.clues: A check engine light, or rough running in the days before.

causes.name: Security system blocking the start
causes.clues: A key or lock light on the dash.

you: Listen for the fuel pump hum.
Look for a flashing key or security light.

result.title: Starts then stalls: check the key system first, then idle and fuel delivery
result.now: Look for a flashing key or security light right after it stalls, and try the spare key. If that doesn't help, have the car checked before relying on it.
if: If it stalls while you're driving, not just at startup, don't drive it. When the engine stalls, steering and braking can take much more force, which is dangerous in traffic.
If you smell fuel, stop trying to start it and look for a leak.
result.why: When a car fires up and dies within seconds, the security system is often letting it start and then cutting fuel because it doesn't recognize the key. If the key is fine, the idle control or fuel delivery may not be keeping it running.

causes.name: Immobilizer not recognizing the key
causes.clues: A key or security light, or it happens with one key but not the other.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: The idle has been low or uneven.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump or clogged filter
causes.clues: Sputtering or hesitation when you press the gas.

you: Watch for a security light.
Try the spare key.

result.title: Cold-start stalling often points to idle control or a sensor reading wrong
result.now: Let it idle for 30 seconds before driving off on cold mornings, and book a check.
if: If the check engine light comes on or it starts stalling when warm too, get it checked sooner.
If it stalls while you're moving, pull over when it is safe and don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking can take much more force when the engine stalls.
result.why: A cold engine needs extra fuel and a higher idle. If a temperature sensor gives the computer the wrong reading, or the idle system is dirty, the engine can die until it warms up. Live sensor data at a shop usually shows which.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control valve
causes.clues: A low, uneven idle.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge acts oddly, or fuel economy has dropped.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a rough idle that smooths out when warm.

you: Note the outside temperature when it happens.
Listen for hissing from the engine bay.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: The idle may be too low to handle extra load
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days. Don't hold the gas to keep it running while you shift into gear, because the car can lurch.
if: If it stalls while driving or as you come to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking can take much more force when the engine stalls.
If the check engine light is steady, have the code read before driving further. If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: Shifting into gear or turning on the A/C adds load to the engine. If the idle control can't raise the engine speed to match, the engine stumbles and dies.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: The idle drops noticeably when the A/C kicks on.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Torque converter clutch not releasing (automatic)
causes.clues: It stalls when coming to a stop, like stalling a manual car.

you: Notice whether the A/C makes the stall more likely.

result.title: Let a shop or roadside service take a look
result.now: Note anything you see or hear when you try to start it, then call roadside assistance or have it towed to a shop.
if: If you smell fuel or burning, stop trying to start it.
result.why: Without knowing whether there's power and whether the engine turns over, it's hard to narrow it down safely. A technician can check the battery, starter and fuel in a few minutes.

causes.name: Battery or connection problem
causes.clues: The most common cause of a no-start.

causes.name: Starter problem
causes.clues: A click with no crank.

causes.name: Fuel or ignition problem
causes.clues: It cranks but won't run.

you: Record a short video with sound of what happens when you try to start it. It helps the shop a lot.
